translation_en: Jabir ibn Abdullah reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “Whoever gives a lifetime grant to a man and his descendants, it belongs to him and his descendants.” This wording is narrated by Yahya ibn Yahya and Muhammad ibn Rumh from al-Layth, and by Qutaybah from Layth, through Ibn Shihab, Abu Salamah, and Jabir. Yahya’s version begins: “Any man who is given a lifetime grant, it belongs to him and his descendants.”

Jabir reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “If a man gives another a lifetime grant for him and his descendants, saying, ‘I give it to you and your descendants as long as any of you remains,’ it belongs to the recipient and will not return to its owner, because it was a gift subject to inheritance.” The report is transmitted through Abd al-Rahman ibn Bishr, Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Shihab, and Abu Salamah, from Jabir al-Ansari.

Jabir said that the lifetime grant approved by the Messenger of Allah was one in which the giver said, “It is yours and your descendants’.” But if he said, “It is yours for as long as you live,” it returned to the giver. Maamar said al-Zuhri gave legal rulings according to this.

Jabir reported that the Messenger of Allah ruled that a lifetime grant to a man and his descendants belonged to them outright; the giver could not impose a condition or retain a portion. Abu Salamah explained that the gift was subject to inheritance, which ended the giver’s condition. Abu Salamah explained that inheritance applies to this gift and cancels the giver’s condition.

This is the same account transmitted by Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna through Abd al-Ala, Hisham, Muhammad, and Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman. Three of Saad ibn Malik’s children each related it with wording like Amr ibn Said’s report: Saad fell ill in Makkah and the Prophet came to visit him.

After the woman and her son died, the son’s child claimed that the garden returned to their family. The giver’s sons said it had belonged to their father for life and after death. They disputed before Tariq, freedman of Uthman, who called Jabir to testify. Jabir testified to the Prophet’s ruling that a lifetime grant belongs to its recipient. Tariq ruled for the recipient’s sons, informed Abd al-Malik, and Abd al-Malik affirmed that Jabir had spoken truthfully. The garden has remained with those sons ever since.

The transmitters are Abu Kamil al-Jahdari from Hammad ibn Zayd; Zuhayr ibn Harb from Ismail ibn Ulayyah; Abu al-Tahir from Ibn Wahb and Yunus; Harun ibn Said from Ibn Wahb and Usamah ibn Zayd al-Laythi; and Muhammad ibn Rafi from Ibn Abi Fudayk and Hisham ibn Sad. All report it from Nafi, from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet. Their wordings differ: most say that he has something to bequeath, while Ayyub’s version says he intends to bequeath, matching Yahya’s narration.

Ibn Umar said that from the night he heard the Messenger of Allah say this, he never spent a night without his will written and kept with him.

Saad ibn Abi Waqqas said: “During the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Messenger of Allah came to visit me because of an illness that brought me close to death. I said, ‘Messenger of Allah, you see how ill I am. I have wealth, and only one daughter will inherit from me. May I give two-thirds of my wealth in charity?’ He said, ‘No.’ I asked, ‘Then half?’ He said, ‘No.’ I asked, ‘Then one-third?’ He said, ‘One-third, and one-third is much. It is better for you to leave your heirs wealthy than to leave them dependent, begging from people. You will be rewarded for every spending you make seeking Allah’s pleasure, even the morsel you put in your wife’s mouth.’ I said, ‘Messenger of Allah, will I remain behind my companions?’ He said, ‘You will not remain and do a deed seeking Allah’s pleasure without gaining in rank and honor. Perhaps you will remain until some people benefit through you and others are harmed by you. O Allah, complete my companions’ migration for them and do not make them turn back.’ But the unfortunate one is Saad ibn Khawlah.” The Messenger of Allah expressed sorrow that Saad ibn Khawlah had died in Makkah. This report is transmitted by Yahya ibn Yahya from Ibrahim ibn Sad and Ibn Shihab, from Amir ibn Sad, from his father.

Three of Saad ibn Malik’s children each related it with wording like Amr ibn Said’s report: Saad fell ill in Makkah and the Prophet came to visit him. Three of Saad’s children each reported from their father that the Prophet visited him in Makkah while he was ill. Saad wept, saying he feared dying in the land from which he had emigrated, as Saad ibn Khawlah had. The Prophet asked why he was weeping, then prayed three times, “O Allah, heal Saad.” Saad said, “Messenger of Allah, I have much property, and only my daughter will inherit from me. May I bequeath all my property?” The Prophet said no. Saad asked about two-thirds, then half, and the Prophet refused each time. When Saad asked about one-third, the Prophet said, “One-third, and one-third is much. Your charity from your wealth is charity, your spending on your family is charity, and what your wife eats from your wealth is charity. Leaving your family well-off, or living comfortably, is better than leaving them begging from people.” The Prophet gestured with his hand. The chain is Muhammad ibn Abi Umar, al-Thaqafi, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Amr ibn Said, Humayd al-Himyari, and three of Saad’s children.

Ibn Abbas said: ‘If people reduced a bequest from one-third to one-quarter, that would be better, for the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: One-third, and one-third is much.’ Waki’s version says: Great or much. The report is transmitted by Ibrahim ibn Musa al-Razi, Isa ibn Yunus, Waki, Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Kurayb, Ibn Numayr, Hisham ibn Urwah, his father, and Ibn Abbas.
